# Evaluated Applications — full package docs

This file concatenates the plain-text content of every published Evaluated Applications package's
owner-authored source doc (`MonoRepo/<Pkg>/docs/site.md`), verbatim except for markdown-to-plain
reflow. It exists so an AI system can read every package's own words in one request instead of
crawling eleven pages. Each package's own page (linked below) may present this same content with
additional design/rendering; the words below are the package owner's source of truth. Everything
described below is free on NuGet — no paid tier, no license gate on any capability named here.

See https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/llms.txt for the short summary, tool list, and our
partnership offer (we pay third parties to build on this stack).

================================================================================
# Phasor — EvaluatedApplications.Phasor
Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/phasor.html
Install: dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.Phasor
================================================================================

Encode numbers and symbols as phasor faces, then compose them with one algebra instead of a
calculator.

Phasor is a Vector Symbolic Architecture (VSA) codec for .NET. It represents tokens (numbers and
text) as bundles of unit complex numbers called phasors. Composition (bind), decomposition
(unbind), superposition (bundle), and readout (correlation) form the complete algebra; arithmetic
is encoding, not calculation.

The problem it solves: symbolic and numeric data are usually kept separate — numbers flow through
arithmetic circuits, symbols through lookup tables. Phasor bridges them. Bind two numbers on the
linear band and you add them; bind on the log band and you multiply them. A symbol encodes to a
fixed random phasor. Now both live in the same algebra: you can store them together, mix them, and
read values back by correlation. This is the substrate for exact storage (no floating-point error
in bundle/delete), similarity search at scale, and models that reason over both values and symbols
with the same composition operators.

How it works: Encode — a number becomes a face with its value encoded as phase (deterministic); a
symbol gets a salted hash-based random signature. Compose — bind (complex multiply per component)
builds relationships; bundle (sum) collects sets or superpositions; unbind (conjugate) extracts
parts exactly; readout by correlation gives a dot-product score. On the linear band, bind is
addition; on the log band, it's multiplication — arithmetic IS the composition.

Two profiles: PhasorCodec is fixed-width (256 reals) with a frozen identity prefix and a learned
orbital tail, built for neural models. HoloCodec is configurable width, SIMD (Vector<double>), a
planar layout, and a memoized number cache, built for holographic storage and similarity search at
scale. Do not mix faces between the two.

The Hologram type wraps a phasor face and applies the algebra through operators (*, +, /, ~) for
readability and prototyping; in-place static methods (BindInto, BundleInto, UnbindInto) are for hot
loops (operators allocate; measured ~1.7x slower at d=64-96).

Version: 1.3.0.

Minimal example:
```csharp
using Phasor;

double[] five = PhasorCodec.Encode("5");
double[] greeting = PhasorCodec.Encode("hello");
double[] five_plus_three = PhasorCodec.Bind(five, PhasorCodec.Encode("3"));
int sum = PhasorCodec.DecodeSum(five_plus_three, max: 10); // sum == 8
double[] pair = PhasorCodec.Bundle(greeting, five);
double[] extracted = PhasorCodec.Unbind(pair, greeting);  // extracted is close to five
```

Key features: one algebra with no special cases; exact composition (bundle/unbind are exact,
subtraction removes a contribution with no floating-point error); two profiles for different
workloads; no dependencies beyond System/System.Numerics; AOT and trim compatible; deterministic
(not cryptographic) hashing; a memoized decode cache.

Compatibility: .NET 8.0 and 10.0, Windows/Linux/macOS, no platform-specific code, dependency-free.
License: source-available; every capability is free to use.

================================================================================
# EvalApp — EvaluatedApplications.EvalApp
Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/evalapp.html
Install: dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.EvalApp
================================================================================

A self-tuning, resource-gated async pipeline runtime for .NET — describe a process as data and
steps, and stop hand-writing concurrency coordination.

What it does: EvalApp replaces the plumbing every real async .NET codebase ends up writing by
hand — a SemaphoreSlim to stop a flood of requests hammering a database, a guessed constant for
"how many things run at once," a Task.WhenAll wrapped in try/catch to aggregate failures, a
rollback path bolted on after something breaks halfway through. You describe a process as a plain
data record and a sequence of steps; EvalApp compiles that into a single, reusable execution path,
gates every resource it touches (CPU, network, disk, database, or a custom pool) at a real bound,
and — when you turn tuning on — discovers the concurrency that actually works on the hardware it's
running on. It's the shared runtime under every Evaluated Applications product, and it works
standalone: no broker, no external service, no config store.

Why it's useful: one in-process dependency instead of a stack (DI container + MediatR + Polly + TPL
Dataflow); the tuner is proactive, continuously probing for the operating point that keeps things
from breaking rather than reacting after something breaks; whole categories of coordination bugs
don't compile (a saga must close before the pipeline builds; a side-effecting step can't be added
without declaring its resource); the builder chain reads like the process it describes; nothing to
stand up first.

Current version: 1.7.0 — targets net8.0 and net10.0, binary-only, zero dependencies.

Key features: fluent pipeline builder; resource-gated concurrency; adaptive and Bayesian tuning;
parallel ForEach and parallel branches; sagas with compensation; middleware (retry, timeout,
circuit breaker, timing, audit, validation); results as data (PipelineResult<T>), not exceptions;
an offline licensing facade (ECDsa P-256, no network call, ever).

Useful to know: everything in EvalApp is free to use today — nothing is license-gated, and no
capability is capped by tier. Compatibility: .NET 8 and .NET 10, no third-party package references.

Minimal example:
```csharp
using EvalApp.Consumer;

public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New");

Eval.App("Orders")
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .AddStep("Validate", d => d with { Status = "Validated" })
            .AddStep("ApplyDiscount", d => d with { Total = d.Total * 0.9m })
            .AddStep("Complete", d => d with { Status = "Complete" })
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build(); // no license key needed — nothing is license-gated today

var result = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Alice", 99.99m));
```
Build the pipeline once (e.g. at startup); call RunAsync many times.

Design first, code second: decide the data record before touching the builder. Where it doesn't
fit: long-running workflows that must survive a process restart over hours/days are Temporal's job;
purely reactive resilience is what Polly is for. EvalApp is for throughput-sensitive work with no
infrastructure to stand up and concurrency that should tune itself.

================================================================================
# EvalApp.Neural — EvaluatedApplications.EvalApp.Neural
Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/evalapp-neural.html
Install: dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.EvalApp.Neural
================================================================================

Real-time neural tuning for data-parallel pipelines.

Problem: EvalApp's built-in concurrency tuner works well on clean, predictable workloads but falls
flat when conditions shift or gates couple (database racing CPU racing disk). You either tune once
and hope, or freeze the tuning and regret it later.

Solution: EvalApp.Neural plugs a tiny, always-learning neural policy into EvalApp in place of the
heuristic. It trains on a real workload's own experience, so it adapts live as conditions change.
Ships warm (pre-trained on diverse scenarios) and keeps learning from every decision. Fast (about
0.4ms per decision) and low overhead.

Why it works: online learning reacts to real-time shifts a frozen heuristic can't; matches the
built-in heuristic on lean/obvious pipelines (no edge there) but beats it roughly 25% on coupled
multi-gate benchmarks; opt-in with no refactor — add .WithNeuralTuning() to the app builder.

Version: v1.0.1.

How to use:
```csharp
var app = Eval.App(...).WithResource(...).WithNeuralTuning().DefineDomain(...);
```
Install it globally for every app:
```csharp
using var _ = NeuralTuning.UseGlobally(NeuralTuning.NewModel());
```
Or train on your own workload by pointing a shared model file at every runner:
```csharp
using var _ = NeuralTuning.UseGloballyPersisted("model.bin");
```

Key features: warm-start (ships pre-trained, nothing to configure); always learning (real-time
adaptation, no manual retuning); tiny footprint (a small holographic model via AlgFormer, roughly
0.4ms/decision); no license gate — runs at full effect regardless of license tier; production ready
(coordinate descent for multi-gate coupling, deterministic under a repeated seed).

What you need to know: best on coupled/noisy workloads — clean single-gate CPU-bound pipelines
won't see much gain. Depends on EvalApp and AlgFormer (bundled, no separate install). Compatible
with .NET 8.0+, Windows/Linux.

================================================================================
# AlgFormer — EvaluatedApplications.AlgFormer
Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/algformer.html
Install: dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.AlgFormer
================================================================================

A transformer engine with two interchangeable attention cores — one classic, one holographic — in
pure managed code, no external ML runtime.

AlgFormer is a .NET library for defining, training, and running transformer-style language models.
Give it a vocabulary and a shape, train it on your own token sequences through a data-parallel
pipeline, and run inference (single prediction, full logits, or streaming generation with a KV
cache).

The problem it solves: most transformer tooling means either binding into a native runtime (ONNX,
PyTorch/libtorch, CUDA) or hand-rolling matrix code with no attention research behind it. AlgFormer
sits in between: a real, gradient-trained transformer architecture, written entirely in C# as
double[] arrays with SIMD, that runs anywhere .NET runs, with no GPU, no Python, and no native
binary to ship. It also lets you compare two ideas of what "attention" should cost. Standard
softmax attention scores every token against every other token — quadratic in sequence length.
AlgFormer ships a second, holographic attention core alongside it that composes context through
bind/bundle/unbind operations instead — linear in sequence length, with constant-time-per-token
serving.

Why it's useful: two real cores (AlgFormer softmax, HoloFormer holographic) sharing the same model
shape, training loop, checkpoint format, and serving API; no external ML runtime; attention that
scales differently (HoloFormer is O(T·d) to train, effectively O(1) per token to serve, versus
O(T²·d) for standard attention); a subword tokenizer, data-parallel trainer, streaming generation
with a KV cache, checkpoint save/load with format versioning, and helpers to grow a trained model
to a longer context or bigger vocabulary; distributed/swarm training over MQTT.

Current version: 2.13.0 (per package CLAUDE.md as of this writing; check the package page's own
version pill for the exact live figure).

Minimal example:
```csharp
using PrismFormer;

var model = new AlgFormer(vocab: 16, shifts: 4, layers: 2, maxContext: 6, dModel: 32, frozenPrefix: 0);

var data = new List<(int[] Ctx, int Target)>
{
    (new[] { 1, 2, 3 }, 4),
    (new[] { 2, 3, 4 }, 5),
};
var trainer = new PrismTrainer(model); // data-parallel via EvalApp
double loss = trainer.TrainEpoch(data, batchSize: 2, lr: 5e-2, shuffleSeed: 1);

var context = new[] { 1, 2, 3 };
int next = model.Predict(context);
double[] logits = model.LogitsFor(context);
int[] generated = model.Generate(context, maxNewTokens: 5, temperature: 0.8, seed: 1);
```
Swapping in the holographic core is the same shape — construct a HoloFormer instead of an
AlgFormer with matching dimensions.

Compatibility: .NET 8 and .NET 10, pure managed code, no native dependencies. Depends on the
Phasor codec package and the EvalApp pipeline runtime; swarm relay components use MQTTnet.
License: proprietary, compiled library only; every capability described is free to use today.

================================================================================
# AlgFormer.Gpu — EvaluatedApplications.AlgFormer.Gpu
Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/algformer-gpu.html
Install: dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.AlgFormer.Gpu
================================================================================

Optional GPU acceleration for AlgFormer's HoloFormer engine — same model, same weights, just
faster.

What it does: AlgFormer.Gpu adds ILGPU/CUDA-backed training and inference for the HoloFormer
(resonator/holographic attention) engine from the core AlgFormer package. It builds GPU kernels
straight from a CPU HoloFormer's serialized weights — no separate model format, no retraining to
switch devices. Backward passes, the fused on-device Adam optimizer step, and batched forward
inference all run on the GPU when one is present, with the CPU engine automatically taking over
when it isn't.

Why it's useful: drop-in, not a rewrite (point it at an existing CPU HoloFormer, it trains/serves
against the same serialized weights); automatic fallback (the same build works on a machine with a
CUDA GPU and one without); correctness-checked against the CPU engine (every GPU kernel is
gradient-checked against the CPU HoloFormer's double-precision math as the reference oracle — GPU
runs in float32 for speed, so results are float-close, not bit-identical); fused on-device Adam
avoiding a CPU round trip on every training batch.

Current version: 1.3.0 (NuGet: EvaluatedApplications.AlgFormer.Gpu).

Key features: GPU-batched forward and backward training for HoloFormer, including per-layer
weight-tied iterative refinement ("StackIter") and all-positions loss; fused on-device Adam
optimizer step plus checkpoint/resume of the GPU-resident optimizer state; automatic device
detection (GpuDevice.HasGpu) with silent, safe CPU fallback; standalone kernel verification
utilities.

Good to know: requires an ILGPU-supported CUDA device at runtime to actually use the GPU path,
otherwise falls back to CPU automatically. Optional — the core AlgFormer package has no GPU
dependency at all and stays dependency-free and AOT/trim-safe. Also includes GPU support for
AlgFormer's earlier (non-HoloFormer) softmax-attention model, which is deprecated — new projects
should use the HoloFormer path. Requires the core EvaluatedApplications.AlgFormer package
alongside it.

NOTE: this package's owner-authored site.md does not include a minimal code sample; none is
invented here. See the API description above and the package's own CLAUDE.md for exact call
shapes, or ask the package owner for one.

================================================================================
# HoloDb — EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb
Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holodb/
Install: dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb
================================================================================

One store. Query it by key, by content, or by aggregate.

What it is: HoloDb is an embeddable, transactional SQL database for .NET that stores data as
holograms in a single associative store. Every value is encoded as a phase vector, and a row's
columns are bound into one hologram — so the same copy of the data can be retrieved three ways:
exact lookup by primary key (ordinary SQL), similarity search by content (NEAREST), and
constant-time analytics that read a maintained total instead of scanning. Most databases bolt a
separate vector index and a separate analytical cube onto a row store and keep all three in sync.
HoloDb keeps one copy and answers all three kinds of question against it.

The problem it solves: applications that need relational storage, similarity/vector search, and
fast dashboard rollups normally reach for three different systems and pay the integration cost of
keeping them consistent. HoloDb collapses that into one embeddable .NET package with real ACID
guarantees.

Why it's useful: no separate vector index (NEAREST ranks rows by resemblance, in SQL, over the same
table); aggregates don't scan (a column's running total is itself a maintained vector, so
COUNT/SUM/MIN/MAX and single-column GROUP BY are constant time); real ACID (write-ahead logging,
bounded crash recovery, reader/writer locking, atomic statements); survives partial loss by design
(columns are the source of truth, holograms are always derivable from them); scales past RAM
(paged tables with a buffer pool + write-ahead log); stays fast under live ingest (reads served from
a snapshot republished after each write, without the write lock).

Current version: 1.10.0 (EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb on NuGet).

Minimal example:
```csharp
using HoloDb;

var db = new HoloDbService(new HoloDbOptions { WalPath = "app.wal" });
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, age INT, name TEXT)");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 30, 'Ada')");

var result = await db.ExecuteAsync("SELECT name FROM users WHERE age >= 18");
foreach (var row in result.Rows) Console.WriteLine(row["name"]);
```
Register with DI via services.AddHoloDb(), or attach to an EvalApp pipeline with
builder.WithHoloDb(service).

Anything else worth knowing: every capability is free to use, nothing gated behind a tier or a
license key. No UPSERT (insert on an existing primary key always throws). One primary key per
table, no outer joins yet. Ships as a compiled library only; source is proprietary. HoloDb is plain
managed .NET with no native dependencies, so the exact same package runs unmodified inside a Blazor
WebAssembly app in a visitor's browser tab.

================================================================================
# HoloDb.Client — EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Client
Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holodb-client.html
Install: dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Client
================================================================================

A .NET client library for remote HoloDb database servers over TLS.

What it does: HoloDb.Client connects your .NET app to a HoloDb server over TCP with mandatory TLS
encryption and token authentication. Run SQL queries and bulk-load data using the same API as the
embedded in-process HoloDbService, so you can swap from embedded to networked by changing only how
you create the handle. Columnar results stay columnar on the wire — no row buffering or JSON
serialization overhead.

The problem: building analytics or database-driven apps means choosing between speed (embed the
database in-process) and scalability (run it on its own server). This library lets you have both.

Why HoloDb.Client: same API embedded or networked (Execute, ExecuteAsync, BulkLoadAsync,
GetStatsAsync, PingAsync); columnar over the wire (typed column arrays, matching the in-process
engine's QueryResult shape); secure by default (TLS on, trust a self-signed server via a pinned
thumbprint or skip it in dev only); built-in resilience (v1.4.0 — optional exponential backoff with
full jitter, a circuit breaker, and a per-operation deadline budget); designed for concurrency (one
client per worker, or pool clients with HoloDbClientPool).

Version: 1.4.0 — adds operation deadline budgets across retries and circuit-breaker state; v1.3.0
added a circuit breaker; v1.2.0 switched to exponential backoff.

Minimal example:
```csharp
using HoloDb.Client;

var client = await HoloDbClient.ConnectAsync("db.example.com", 5433);
try {
    var result = await client.ExecuteAsync("SELECT id, value FROM data LIMIT 10");
    foreach (var row in result.Rows) {
        Console.WriteLine($"id={row[0]}, value={row[1]}");
    }
} finally {
    await client.DisposeAsync();
}
```

Requirements: .NET 8.0 or .NET 10.0; a HoloDb server v1.4.0+ (wire-protocol compatible); network
connectivity to the server with TLS support. One client = one session (requests serialize through
an internal queue). License: proprietary, part of Evaluated Applications, free to use.

================================================================================
# HoloDb.Protocol — EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Protocol
Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holodb-protocol.html
Install: dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Protocol
================================================================================

A columnar wire protocol: the contract between HoloDb server and client, keeping column-oriented
performance alive on the wire.

What it does: HoloDb.Protocol defines how the HoloDb server and client communicate. Instead of
sending results as JSON or row-by-row data structures, it preserves the columnar shape: a long[],
double[], or string[] travels as a typed array over the wire. Handles length-prefixed TCP framing,
a binary columnar codec, request/response dispatch (Hello/Exec/BulkLoad/Stats/Ping), version
negotiation, and error semantics that distinguish protocol errors from query errors.

Why it matters: most database protocols trade columnar performance for JSON or ORM convenience;
this protocol keeps the columnar win alive all the way to the client, and encodes the wire format
explicitly (predictable, versionable, testable).

Current version: 1.0.2 (.NET 8.0 / 10.0, nullable-enabled).

How to get it: normally pulled in transitively via EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Client. If you are
implementing a server (or working on HoloDb's server code), depend on this package directly.

Minimal example (server-side, using this package to build a server):
```csharp
var payload = await Wire.ReadFrameAsync(networkStream);
var request = HoloProtocol.DecodeRequest(payload);

if (request.Op == WireOp.Exec)
{
    var result = await engine.ExecuteAsync(request.Sql);
    var response = HoloProtocol.Result(result);
    await Wire.WriteFrameAsync(networkStream, response);
}
```
Client-side, use HoloDb.Client instead, which wraps this protocol.

Compatibility & wire stability: the wire format is frozen — opcode byte values never change,
message field order and types are stable. Most consumers should depend on HoloDb.Client instead;
depend on this package directly only if implementing a server.

================================================================================
# HoloVoxel — EvaluatedApplications.HoloVoxel
Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holovoxel.html
Install: dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloVoxel
================================================================================

A holographic voxel engine for .NET where level-of-detail isn't a mesh trick, it's how reading the
world works.

What it does: most voxel engines store a world as arrays of blocks and fake distant detail with
mesh simplification, mipmaps, or LOD popping. HoloVoxel stores a chunk of the world as one
holographic superposition instead: every voxel is bound (position ⊗ content) and summed into a
single vector, using the Phasor VSA codec. Reading a voxel back is a correlation against that
vector, and correlating with fewer components gives a cheaper, fuzzier answer — near stays crisp,
far goes soft, with no discrete LOD tiers and no popping between them. The engine also exposes a
decoded-confidence signal a renderer can map to visual solidity.

Why it's different: LOD is free (no separate simplified mesh to generate, store, or stitch);
memory scales with perceived detail, not world size (a chunk only stores as many components as its
LOD will ever need, losslessly up to that budget); the blur is honest, not aesthetic (distant
terrain looks soft because the engine genuinely has less information at that budget); engine only,
plug into anything (no rendering or graphics dependency, verified headless).

Current version: 1.5.0 (EvaluatedApplications.HoloVoxel on NuGet).

Key features: holographic chunk storage (HoloWorld, Chunk) decodable at any component budget as a
colour field or a triangulated surface mesh with analytic per-vertex normals; continuous, meshless
LOD; field confidence for adaptive detail; spatial coarsening at distance; truncated holograms
(storage cost tracks the LOD budget you plan to read at); fused SIMD bind/correlate; entities too
(HoloModel stores a creature or prop the same holographic way); a built-in procedural world
generator, or supply your own world source; a ringworld warp on top of the same flat chunk storage.

Good to know: this is the engine, not the renderer — HoloVoxel has no graphics dependency and is
verified headless, handing you decoded colour fields, meshes, and confidence values; drawing them
is up to the consuming front end. Built on Phasor. No license gate — every capability is free to
use, DLL-only distribution, proprietary license.

NOTE: this package's owner-authored site.md does not include a minimal code sample; none is
invented here. See the API description above and the package's own CLAUDE.md for exact call
shapes, or ask the package owner for one.

# Prose — EvaluatedApplications.Prose
Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/prose.html
Install: dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.Prose
================================================================================

A grammar-driven synthetic corpus generator for .NET.

What it is: Prose reads plain text through the rules of grammar, keeps what it learns in a HoloDb
database, and recombines that knowledge into new sentences that are grammatical, use words suited
to their slots, and read plausibly. It exists to grow a training corpus: mine the grammatical
knowledge already in your text (which nouns, verbs and adjectives go together, and how), then
generate more of it, along with question/answer pairs for reading-comprehension training data.

The problem it solves: language models need volume and variety of grammatically correct text.
Hand-writing or scraping more data doesn't scale, and most "data augmentation" either pastes
fragments together ungrammatically or needs its own large model to run. Prose parses real text
into its grammatical structure with deterministic rules, stores what nouns/verbs/adjectives
actually co-occur with what, and recombines those attested pieces into fresh sentences guaranteed
to parse correctly before they're ever written out.

Why it's different: rules-first, not model-first (a small optional language model can rank
candidates by plausibility, but Prose degrades gracefully to pure rules with no model at all); no
word is locked to one role (the same surface form resolves to noun or verb by context, e.g. "the
panda eats shoots and leaves" vs "the panda eats, shoots, and leaves" — punctuation and structure
alone flip the reading, and Prose gets both right); nothing imaginary (every open-class word Prose
emits is a form it actually observed in the source text); handles real grammatical structure
(indirect objects, relative clauses, multi-sentence passages with coreference), not just word
salad.

Current version: 1.1.0 (NuGet package EvaluatedApplications.Prose).

Key features: parse (sentence splitting, POS tagging, phrase chunking, role assignment, zero
training, no external model); mine (builds a lexicon plus selectional tables in a HoloDb database);
generate (samples a sentence shape, fills each slot with an attested agreement-correct word, keeps
only sentences that re-parse validly); optional plausibility scoring; Q&A generation (single-
sentence, multi-sentence passages with coreference, self-referential two-turn dialogues); corpus
and TSV export.

Minimal example:
```csharp
var prose = new ProseEngine();
prose.Mine(@"C:\corpus\text");                 // parse every *.txt and mine it
prose.Save(@"prose.wal");                       // persist the mined tables (optional)

foreach (var sentence in prose.Generate(1000))  // new, grammatical, plausible sentences
    Console.WriteLine(sentence);

prose.WriteCorpus(@"C:\corpus\synthetic", 100_000);  // write sentences out as .txt for an LM
prose.WriteQaPairs(@"C:\corpus\qa", 50_000);          // context+question -> answer TSV
```
Parse a single sentence directly, no mining or database required:
```csharp
var p = ProseEngine.ParseSentence("The panda eats, shoots, and leaves.");
Console.WriteLine(ProseEngine.Explain(p));   // subject, verbs, objects, template
```

Good to know: depends on two other Evaluated Applications packages, HoloDb (storage engine) and
AlgFormer (optional plausibility-scoring model) — installing this package pulls both in
automatically. Ships as a compiled library; every capability is free to use under a proprietary
license.

================================================================================
# Tracer — EvaluatedApplications.Tracer
Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/tracer.html
Install: dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.Tracer
================================================================================

Navmesh pathfinding and game AI for .NET: multi-agent path queries, dynamic obstacles,
line-of-sight, and combat, all self-tuning to your frame budget.

Tracer is a pathfinding and game-AI SDK for real-time simulations with many moving agents: crowds,
RTS-style unit groups, tactical squads. It bakes triangle-based navmeshes, routes single agents and
whole swarms across them, reacts to obstacles that appear or vanish mid-game, and layers the
surrounding game-AI toolkit (line-of-sight, fog-of-war, influence maps, combat engagement) on top.

The problem it solves: most pathfinding libraries stop at "find me a path." Real games need a lot
more: hundreds of agents converging on the same goal without re-solving the same route hundreds of
times; obstacles that block and unblock at runtime without a full re-bake; visibility and cover
queries for AI perception; a frame-time budget the pathfinder has to live inside of. Tracer builds
all of that in as one coherent SDK, running on a data-parallel pipeline (EvalApp) that tunes its
own concurrency to the workload.

What it does: navmesh baking (with obstacle-polygon exclusion, optional hierarchical bake); single-
and multi-agent pathfinding (goal-sharing so agents converging on one point reuse the same solve);
dynamic obstacles (block/unblock at runtime without a full re-bake); line-of-sight, fog-of-war,
influence maps; combat engagement (spatial-hashed, pluggable damage/dodge/block formulas); steering
behaviors (Seek, Wander, Patrol, Flee, Queue, FlowLane); grid tactics (a separate, bake-free lane
for tile/square-grid tactics games); adaptive path budgeting under a tight frame budget.

Version: current 1.2.0.

Minimal example:
```csharp
using Tracer;

var world = new PathfindingWorld();

var baker = world.CreateNavMeshBakerService();
var mesh = await baker.BakeAsync(vertices, triangleIndices);

var single = world.CreateSingleAgentService();
var waypoints = await single.QueryPathAsync(mesh, start, goal);

var multi = world.CreateMultiAgentService();
var result = await multi.TickAsync(agents, mesh, tickNumber: 0);
```

What you need to know: depends on EvalApp (self-tuning concurrency for every heavy tick) and
Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Abstractions. Target .NET 8.0 and .NET 10.0. License:
proprietary; every capability is free to use today, nothing gated behind a tier or a license key.
Proven in use building the Eden game project (navmesh movement, perception/fog, combat resolution,
tactical squad control).
